newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-FORECAST-Australia c/a deficit steady in July.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-FORECAST-Australia c/a deficit steady in July.

text.p: Australia's current account deficit for July is expected to be close to the favourable June result, but long term nature of the deficit problem was reinforced by the budget forecast of no improvement in the coming year, economists said.

Economists generally expect Thursday's data to be comfortably below A$1.5 billion, but the wild card is the inclusion of updated information from the June quarter survey of foreign investment investment, which will be included in this release.
"We're expecting quite a good current account outcome this month," ANZ Treasury economist David de Garis said.
The median forecast of the 27 economists Reuters surveyed ahead of Thursday's data is for a July current account deficit of A$1.3 billion, essentially unchanged from June's A$1.291 billion shortfall.
Forecasts ranged from A$1.1 billion to A$1.6 billion, with the already published 2.8 percent fall in merchandise imports a key to the expected low July number.

Economists said that fall should counter an expected correction to the strong 4.1 percent rise in June exports, and so the trade balance should remain in surplus for the second consecutive month, something that has not happened since January and February 1994.

"The 2.8 percent fall in imports in July, in combination with a modest fall in exports and a steady net income deficit performance is likely to see a July current account shortfall of around A$1.3 billion," Westpac economist John Peters said.

Despite the deficit improving from over A$2 billion just a few months ago, economists said the monthly deficits had probably improved as far as they could, with the net income deficit placing a monthly floor of A$1.5 billion under it.

"The big element of the current account deficit remains the net income deficit," ANZ's de Garis said, adding it required a large contribution from government savings, with the budget needing to be sustained in surplus for a number of years.
"That clearly requires a big contribution from government savings -- not just to get back into balance, but to actually get it into surplus, and sustain it there over a number of years," he said.
In last week's budget the government forecast a 1996/97 deficit of A$20 billion, or four percent of gross domestic product, little changed from the 1995/96 result.

While the government has announced a fiscal consolidation plan that will return the underlying budget to surplus in 1998/99 and ease pressure on the current account deficit, the results will be a few years coming, economists said.
"I think it's really going to spread out on a longer term basis, over the next few years," AMP Investments chief economist Shane Oliver said.

"Firstly we have to see that fiscal tightening sustained in accordance with the government's projections...and secondly as we learnt in the 1980's there is no one for one relationship between the budget deficit and the current account deficit, so....we wouldn't really be expecting it to result in significant improvements through 1996/97," he said.
